ov: Seven prescribed poems of Rosemary Dobson: ‘Young Girl at a Window’, ‘Summer’s End’, ‘Cock Crow’, ‘A Fine Thing’, ‘Child of Our Time’, ‘Piltdown Man’ and ‘Every Man His Own Sculptor’. This guide covers the first three in depth, because only these were supplied; the other four need their own text and quotes. Dobson’s poems are short, formal and quietly intense. They look at moments of pause (a threshold, a season’s turn, a night walk) to examine time, solitude and the cost of being human.
rub: Language, forms and features: regular stanzas and rhyme, controlled imagery and personification give each poem a calm surface that holds strong feeling.
Identity and choice: ‘Cock Crow’ tests agency (the wish to be alone) against responsibility (mother and daughter).
Endurance: ‘Young Girl at a Window’ pictures life as a journey that ends in “snow”.
sum: ‘Young Girl at a Window’ addresses a girl at a window latch at the end of a day. Time is “killed” or “lost”, the room is watchful, and the final stanza imagines a journey with the eyes over gentle hills, a map of living that leads “through grass and sheaves and, lastly, snow.” ‘Summer’s End’ describes the first wave of winter sweeping summer’s crowds from the beach, then leaves the lonely mermaid who “married a mortal” weeping at the water’s edge. ‘Cock Crow’ follows a speaker who walks a dark road to be “myself, alone”, leaving her sleeping mother and daughter behind. She feels both freedom and guilt and ends with the disillusion of hearing the cock crow three times.
acts: A threshold poem about the end of day, time, loss and the long journey of life.
A seasonal poem that moves from a crowded summer beach to the loneliness of the mermaid who married a mortal.
A night walk between a “lit house” and the town, where a woman tests her need for solitude against love and duty.
ch: The speaker (‘Young Girl at a Window’)
A guiding voice that is part observer, part elder. It gives the girl a map of life and a sense of its end.
This way the map of living lies.
Young, silent and on the verge of life’s journey. She is invited to see time as both loss and a path.
Lift your hand to the window latch.
A lonely outsider who “married a mortal”. She suffers because she belongs to two worlds and neither fully.
Where the sand is like knives to her feet.
A woman who stands between two generations (“one life behind and one before”) and asserts her own self at the cost of guilt.
cx: Rosemary Dobson (1920–2012) was an Australian poet whose work often turns toward painting, myth and the passing of time. In ‘Cock Crow’ the speaker’s position “between” her mother and daughter reflects the generational pressures many women experience. Check your teacher’s notes for the artwork or personal context behind each poem.

Dobson’s poems draw on classical and biblical allusion. The cock crowing three times in ‘Cock Crow’ recalls Peter’s denial of Christ in the New Testament, which gives the poem a moral weight about betrayal and self-knowledge. The mermaid belongs to fairytale and folklore.

Mid-twentieth-century Australia valued the roles of wife and mother. A woman’s wish to be “myself, alone” would have been radical, which is why the speaker feels she has “denied / Their needs”. The poems were written in the shadow of two world wars and the sense of time’s fragility.
Women’s roles in the family, the tension between independence and responsibility, and the loneliness of those who live between two worlds.
im: The window and the latch: a threshold between inner and outer worlds. The girl must choose to open it.
The clock and the “guiltless minute hand”: time as a witness that does not judge, even though “Time was killed”.
The beach and the wave: a wave of winter sweeps away summer’s crowd. Seasonal change shows life’s passing.
The road, the bridge and the dark trees: the speaker’s three walks mark her struggle between freedom and obligation. The cock’s crow recalls betrayal and awareness.
th: Time passes, and every life moves toward its end, here pictured as winter.
Common Module Q2: endurance of the human spirit.
Being alone can be a freedom and a loss. The mermaid and the night-walker both stand apart.
Love and duty bind people, even when they wish to be free.
Common Module: paradoxes of motivation and behaviour.
Dobson’s poems pause to look closely, making ordinary moments carry meaning.
Common Module: the aesthetic qualities of language.
Strength can be a gesture of self-assertion that comes at a price.

{This way the map of living lies|Technique: extended metaphor of a map. Effect: life becomes a path that can be read and followed. Module link: acceptance and growth.}. / And this the journey you must go / Through grass and sheaves and, lastly, snow.

q.m: Common Module: tension between agency and conformity.

A.i: In her poetry, Rosemary Dobson offers audiences opportunities to examine assumptions about human strength and vulnerability by showing that moments of apparent independence and calm are shadowed by loss. Through ‘Cock Crow’, ‘Summer’s End’ and ‘Young Girl at a Window’, Dobson suggests that strength is the capacity to face solitude, time and mortality without illusion. Her controlled, formal voice invites readers to see vulnerability as the cost, and the proof, of being human.
b: Dobson first challenges the assumption that independence is simple strength. In ‘Cock Crow’, the speaker begins with the assertion, “Wanting to be myself, alone”, the participial phrase stating a desire that the comma leaves hesitant. Her act of “shutting-to the door” on “my mother and my daughter”, who represent “one life behind and one before”, shows the personal price of choosing solitude. The balanced parallelism places her between generations, caught between agency and obligation, and the simple ideal of self-assertion becomes a source of guilt.

Dobson then shows that vulnerability is inseparable from belonging. In ‘Summer’s End’, the wave that “sweeps in a flood the sun-hats and the surfboards” personifies winter as a force that clears away human presence, leaving only “the lonely mermaid / Who married a mortal”. The myth conveys the vulnerability of a being who belongs to two worlds, and the simile “where the sand is like knives to her feet” makes her pain physical. The mermaid’s strength lies in her endurance of that pain, but the poem presents her loneliness as the price.

Finally, Dobson suggests that strength lies in accepting what cannot be changed. In ‘Young Girl at a Window’, time is “killed” and “lies dead”, yet the “guiltless minute hand is still”, and the speaker offers the girl a “map of living” that ends “through grass and sheaves and, lastly, snow.” The extended metaphor of a map turns mortality into a path that can be walked, and the sequence of seasonal images reduces a whole life to a cycle. Strength here is clear-eyed acceptance.
A.c: Ultimately, Dobson asks readers to reconsider what strength and vulnerability mean. Across these poems, assertion brings guilt, belonging brings pain, and calm acceptance of time becomes the poet’s kind of courage, showing that to be human is to be both resilient and exposed.
A.n: What to notice: the thesis states a clear argument about strength and vulnerability. Each paragraph is built around one poem and one idea (independence, belonging, acceptance). Quotes are short and embedded; techniques (participial phrase, parallelism, personification, simile, extended metaphor) are named with their effects; the module idea of agency and conformity returns.

B.i: In her poems ‘Cock Crow’, ‘Summer’s End’ and ‘Young Girl at a Window’, Rosemary Dobson shows how strength and vulnerability are connected. The poems explore solitude, time and family.
b: In ‘Cock Crow’, the speaker says, “Wanting to be myself, alone.” This shows that she wants independence. But she leaves her mother and daughter, “shutting-to the door”, which shows she feels guilty. This shows that being independent can make you vulnerable.
In ‘Summer’s End’, the mermaid is “lonely”. The simile “like knives to her feet” shows that she is in pain. This shows that she is vulnerable because she is between two worlds.
In ‘Young Girl at a Window’, Dobson uses the image of a map, “the map of living”, to show that life is a journey that ends in “snow”. This shows that people have to accept that they will die.
B.c: In conclusion, Dobson shows that strength and vulnerability go together. Her poems show that people can be strong by facing loneliness and time.
B.n: What to notice: relevant quotes and a clear point per paragraph. The analysis is brief (“this shows that…”), techniques are named only twice, and “assumptions” in the question is not addressed.

models.C: In Cock Crow the speaker wants to be alone. She leaves her mother and daughter. This shows she is strong but also vulnerable. Dobson uses imagery to show this.
models.D: Cock Crow is about a woman who goes for a walk at night. She is alone. She feels sad.

A.i: Through the particular lives of a night-walking mother, a lonely mermaid and a girl on the threshold of life, Rosemary Dobson’s poetry enriches our understanding of the endurance of the human spirit as the capacity to carry on while knowing the cost. Dobson’s measured stanzas, with their quiet use of metaphor and personification, show endurance as acceptance rather than triumph. Her poems invite readers to value the small, private acts of facing time and solitude.
b: In ‘Cock Crow’, endurance is the choice to live with the consequences of selfhood. The speaker’s “Wanting to be myself, alone” leads her to stand “between”, “one life behind and one before”, and to know herself as “separate and alone, / Cut off from human cries, from pain, / And love that grows about the bone.” The organic metaphor of love growing about the bone makes attachment physical and unavoidable. Her endurance is not heroism but the willingness to return, after the “Too brief illusion”, to the door she closed.

In ‘Summer’s End’, endurance is the mermaid’s patience in loss. After winter’s wave “sweeps in a flood the sun-hats and the surfboards”, the poem leaves “the lonely mermaid / Who married a mortal” weeping where “the sand is like knives to her feet.” The simile makes her suffering sharp and physical, but she remains on the beach, so the spirit endures even where it hurts. Her particular life, divided between two worlds, enriches our understanding of the loneliness behind endurance.

In ‘Young Girl at a Window’, endurance is facing time with open eyes. Time is “killed” and “lies dead”, yet the speaker gives the girl “the map of living” and tells her the journey must be gone “through grass and sheaves and, lastly, snow.” The seasonal sequence turns a whole life into a path to be walked, and the word “lastly” does not avoid the end. The girl’s life is seen from beginning to end, and her spirit endures by knowing where it leads.
A.c: Dobson’s particular figures therefore enrich our understanding of the human spirit’s endurance: it is not the avoidance of loss but the capacity to continue with open eyes. The poems reveal that endurance lives in quiet acceptance, even when it hurts.
A.n: What to notice: “endurance” is defined, and each poem is tied to “particular lives” (speaker, mermaid, girl). Quotes are precise and short; technique and effect are explained in every paragraph.

B.i: In her poems, Rosemary Dobson shows the endurance of the human spirit through the lives of the speaker in ‘Cock Crow’, the mermaid in ‘Summer’s End’ and the girl in ‘Young Girl at a Window’.
b: In ‘Cock Crow’, the speaker wants to be “myself, alone” but is also connected to “love that grows about the bone.” This shows that she cannot escape her family. This shows endurance because she keeps going.
In ‘Summer’s End’, the mermaid is alone on the beach and the sand is “like knives to her feet.” This shows she is in pain but she stays. This shows endurance.
In ‘Young Girl at a Window’, the poem says the journey must go “through grass and sheaves and, lastly, snow.” This shows that life ends but we keep going.
B.c: In conclusion, Dobson shows endurance through the lives of her speakers. They face loneliness and loss but they keep going.
B.n: What to notice: relevant quotes but repetitive explanation (“this shows…”). Little comment on technique or effect, and no direct response to “enriches our understanding”.

fc: What biblical allusion is in ‘Cock Crow’?
The cock crowing three times recalls Peter’s denial of Christ, adding guilt and self-knowledge to the poem.
What does the map metaphor in ‘Young Girl at a Window’ suggest?
Life is a path that can be read and followed, ending in “snow”.
Which simile shows the mermaid’s vulnerability?
“Where the sand is like knives to her feet.”
Which two Dobson poems are most useful for strength and vulnerability?
‘Cock Crow’ (independence and guilt) and ‘Summer’s End’ (the mermaid’s pain).
